We analyze how to identify common stochastic patterns in large datasets that consist of time series, even when the number of series is relatively small. A key challenge in this problem lies in the broad range of possible common patterns. To overcome this, we develop a novel method that takes into account the time component, known as real-time data. Unlike previous methods that can be manipulated by adding or removing data points, our method reliably identifies the main stochastic patterns even with significant changes in data order. Once the patterns are identified, we test for any remaining independent time trends and estimate any common factors based on these results. Notably, the speed of our method does not depend on the size of the dataset, allowing it to effectively handle large data sets. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method performs well in a variety of common cases and even more serious scenarios involving time series. The method is applied to understand the relationship between global stock markets and the S&P 500 index, revealing how global markets have gradually become more interconnected since the late 1990s.

For the first time, a deep imaging survey using the Subaru/SCS on 11 massive galaxy clusters has uncovered 21 instances of multiple lensing effects on galaxies spanning a wide range of redshifts (ranging from1.0 to greater than 6.0). These observations led to the identification of a doubly lensed quasar at a redshift of 6.66, along with three other quasar lensings at redshifts of 6.3, 6.5, and a redshift greater than 6, respectively. Additionally, these discoveries include three of the most distant separately imaged arcs, with redshifts extending to a redshift of 10, on clusters that possess relatively low lensing capabilities. These findings are described in detail.

Internet Service Providers have long been a source of contention due to their monopoly status, with debates surrounding their ability to prioritize content based on profit through targeted advertising. A theoretical model is developed to assess the consequences of profit-sharing agreements between content providers and ISPs. These agreements can lead to higher profits, improved service quality, and increased user demand, with revenue sharing between the two parties. While such arrangements might raise legal and ethical concerns, they present interesting possibilities for design innovation and policy-making.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation of obtaining a state function from a given set of observables. We demonstrate that multiple, distinct approaches can be employed to determine a state when the underlying set of commutative observables - corresponding to individual phases of a system - becomes known.

The $\alpha$-attractor models in inflationary theory hold great promise in the context of upcoming cosmological observations, primarily because their slow-roll parameters are relatively easy to estimate after the end of inflation, resulting in a post-inflationary spectrum of gravitational waves that is relatively hard to detect. To further analyze this, a relatively simple model known as the hybrid $\alpha$-attractor model was studied using Monte Carlo simulations to investigate how future cosmological observations might be able to distinguish between conventional and $\alpha$-attractor models. It became evident, however, that even with advanced space-based detectors, telling these models apart might not be feasible in most cases. Another aspect to consider is their ability to match Planck data, which initial findings suggest could be challenging for these models in some parameter spaces.

In the context of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifold divided into two calibrating regions, marked by the boundary of a geodesic plane, we establish an equivalence between the sets of measured foliations influencing each region's geometry, noted as $M_{\lambda}$ and $M_{\mu}$ respectively. These sets govern the boundary conformal structures of the regions, enabling the definition of a continuous map from one set to the other, denoted as $\Phi: M_{\lambda} \to M_{\mu}$. Our research shows this map is uniformly Lipschitz continuous when the sets are regarded as part of a Teichmüller space, using a specific $L^2$ conformal distance metric.

This study presents a for-profit strategy that selects reference returns to create a portfolio which will yield a higher return than that portfolio on the specified date. Unlike traditional methods that seek to maintain a stable return by referencing a single benchmark or by employing drawdown controls, our approach maintains a small amount of 'excess return' to accelerate growth while controlling losses. The in-sample performance of the strategy can be assessed by dividing it into shorter periods and re-optimizing the strategy for each of these intervals. Since the distribution of portfolio returns over time is unknown, this study utilizes the empirical CDF to estimate it. As a result, this study's findings surpass those obtained from in-sample applications of management techniques that aim to maintain a particular drawdown level. Furthermore, our research employs a unique approach that prescribes the number of periods in the estimation interval as a function of drawdown, thereby ensuring that estimation parameters adjust as a function of portfolio performance. The data used in this study pertains to a for-profit portfolio which was managed between 1986 and 2018 by interviewing top decision makers in the field of finance. The decisions involved in this strategy were made monthly and were based on a search for an 'opportunity return' which was defined as the return of a portfolio of assets selected to meet certain constraints. The strategy was optimized such that the probability of an underperformance relative to a reference return obtained from the CDF was controlled. The decision makers followed this strategy when the estimated

Correct identification of heart conditions necessitates accurate interpretation of sound cues produced by the heart. Consequently, precision in human stethoscope use contributes significantly to disease diagnosis. Nevertheless, there persists a level of human error in this process. This study presents a collaborative system linking a stethoscope to a co-robotic assistant, where the latter poses questions to the human about auditory heart signals for subsequent analysis. This study examines two robotic frameworks - one involving a conversational interface with the human, and another with physical pointing at relevant heart sounds using a robotic arm - to evaluate how each impacts the human's capacity to correctly diagnose cardiac conditions.

We have developed a novel theoretical framework fornwospin-independent parity violation in atomic transitions. Using parity violation electric dipole transitions as an example, we can express the transition amplitude in terms of the electric and magnetic dipole form factors, which are defined within the nucleus rest frame. This formulation enables us to derive a clear relationship between these form factors and the nuclear PV electric dipole form factor, which is a fundamental parameter in the process. Furthermore, we can calculate the matrix elements for the electric and magnetic dipole form factors using consistent effective field theories, both at low and high energy levels. We have also calculated the expectation values of these form factors, both for an odd-proton nucleus with a spinless Z-1 nucleus in the ground state and for a nucleus with an unpolarized neutron, which are essential components in the calculation.

A twist is utilized in the definition of a topological space's K-theory, 
and we examine how this parameter influences its effects. Using a multi-faceted 
approach, we establish a classification system for these influences. 
Furthermore, within each category, we introduce specific elements that can aid in 
distinguishing C*-algebras up to stable isomorphism.

Pomona College's Mathematics & Statistics Department has been dedicated to
establishing an inclusive and welcoming environment for all students to
engage in mathematical study. In response to low diversity among majors, the
department initially attempted to address this through targeted programs aimed
at enhancing students' mathematical abilities. Conversely, recent efforts have
shifted to an anti-deficit strategy, which prioritizes modifying the
department's internal culture to foster a more cohesive community. Our
initiatives to boost collaboration, atmosphere, and overall department
climate are detailed below.

This research focuses on the $H_p$ theory in the context of several complex variables, 
particularly examining properties of the fractional difference operator $\Delta_{h}^{\lambda}$, 
which involves fractional orders. We examine the properties of the operator $T_{j}$ 
given by an infinite series application of the fractional difference operator and 
investigate its mapping between $H_p$ spaces and $\ell_q$ spaces under specific conditions. 
We demonstrate the boundedness of $T_{T}$ from $H_p$ to $\ell_q$ when $1<p<\infty$, 
under the given constraints of $\alpha$ and $r$. We also extend our study to a broader 
scenario, investigating the boundedness of $T_{T}$ from $L_p$ to $ \ell_q$ when $0<p<1$, 
considering certain conditions involving $\alpha$ and $r$.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding strategies and outcome profitability. Through a laboratory experiment where subjects traded a single-item via auctions, we compared the effects of a secret first-price auction and a transparent first-price auction. We found that transparency led to first-price auctions achieving higher outcome profitability. It also revealed that in an opaque environment, strategic bidding was more prevalent. Conversely, in a transparent setting, we observed increased name-bidding and ultimately found no difference in profitability between secret and transparent auctions. Our results emphasize the importance of auction integrity as a design element.

The explanation of accelerated cosmic expansion is crucial in cosmology.
This phenomenon can be partially addressed by a specific type of gravity theory called Symmetric Teleparallel Theory (STT), which incorporates the non-metricity scalar.
To gain a deeper understanding of how STT can naturally accommodate the acceleration of the universe's flat spacetime, researchers analyzed a specific class of solutions known as pp-waves within TGG.
By applying TGG in an arbitrary dimension, they derived a modified form of the Raychaudhuri's equation by considering small perturbations of a specific gravity equation.
These perturbations were then applied to a universally accepted cosmological model, namely the LCDM model, to gain valuable insights into its underlying structure and dynamics.
Ultimately, researchers used the obtained results to calculate a value for the equation for state parameter in this flat spacetime LCDM model by utilizing a specific parameterization of a state parameter in this model, thereby gaining an in-depth understanding of its flat spacetime dynamics.
These state parameter calculations are essential to a broader set of calculations to determine STT's ability to explain the acceleration of the universe's flat spacetime, including its gravity potential and a value for dark energy density.

Research into local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties, specifically for elementary and Borel cases, has been conducted using the parameter space $M_{1,n}$, a specific variant of a tree. This study delves into the local cohomology related to the ideal, particularly its top element, a key component in understanding cutting behaviors. By considering a specific type of variable within the ring, corresponding to vertices on the tree, we can establish an explicit computational method for this cohomology, which then allows us to determine its annihilation. As a result, specific 'geometric vertex decompositions' are introduced, providing insights into how this cohomology is influenced by these geometric structures.

Neural Painters, utilizing a GAN-based approach, generate brushstrokes that are assembled into paintings. Despite GANs' superiority in AI-generated art, their training can be exceptionally challenging. To address these difficulties and accelerate Neural Painter training, we employed Transfer Learning, achieving a notable time reduction from days to just hours without compromising visual quality. Our findings are presented in this study.

We aim to calculate the current sensitivity limit for the CP-violating Kaon decay within the framework of the left-right symmetric model, taking into account recent B-meson decay results. To achieve this, another study should first establish model-sensitive limits on key model parameters, which we take into consideration in the current analysis. The current analysis demonstrates that an enhancement of approximately two orders of magnitude in sensitivity is required for the CP-violating Kaon decay to be detected. This projection is relatively insensitive to variations in the parameter space examined, mainly because the related $K\mu e$ channel significantly suppresses the parameter space at a sensitivity level around $10^{-12}$. The situation changes if the CP-violating Kaon decay becomes the most sensitive probe for CP-violation within the considered parameter space, similar to that for the left-right symmetric model. In such a scenario, the current experiment's sensitivity might not be deep enough to detect the CP-violating Kaon decay.

Academic researchers who read research papers to gain insights into specific topics face a significant barrier, as current systems struggle to translate complex knowledge into answerable formats due to the lack of contextual understanding. This research proposes an innovative approach by developing a new task called Question Localization (QuLoc), which posits that questions cannot be understood in isolation but rather need to be situated within a broader knowledge framework. Building on this hypothesis, a model is introduced that can locate questions within the context of the paper and identify the relevant sections that support or refute a given question. Through extensive experiments on legal and computational topics, the proposed model significantly outperforms traditional approaches that rely on paper representations alone, demonstrating its effectiveness in facilitating new knowledge discovery and paper navigation for researchers.

In order to investigate fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova simulations, we conducted an analysis of MRN14, the most realistic model from the multi-group neutrino transport code ANUE. Our initial examination of the neutrino distribution revealed that in several areas near the neutrino source, an instability could develop. The intensity of this instability depended largely on whether it was a 2D or 3D simulation and was also influenced by the angular resolution. As the simulation progressed and a standing accretion shock formed, an instability emerged in the neutrino source region. Through an examination of the neutrino distribution in both 2D and 3D runs, we discovered that despite differences in neutrino treatment, an instability developed in all cases.

ADHD is a widely prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by inattention and hyperactivity. Although studies into the genetics and neuroscience of ADHD are ongoing, no definitive cause has been identified. Recent research has utilized deep learning to demonstrate the potential of using resting-state functional MRI data for ADHD diagnosis. However, using all brain regions for diagnosis can introduce unnecessary noise and decrease model performance. In this research, we present RSVO, a novel method for selecting the most relevant brain regions for diagnosing ADHD through rsfMRI images. RSVO incorporates regional inhomogeneity into the analysis and uses an entropy-based approach to identify the most informative regions. In a subsequent step, a random forest classifier is employed for final diagnosis. Evaluating RSVO on the publicly available ADHD-200 standalone challenge dataset revealed a 5-point increase in AUC score with reduced computational complexity. Furthermore, our analysis of the chosen regions for our top five models demonstrated superior generalizability and diagnostic capabilities compared to existing research.

In a discrete-time epidemic SISI model where population growth is constant and balanced, the per capita mortality and fertility rates are equivalent, and the model's evolution operator is a nonlinear function of seven parameters. When we reduce this operator to a quadratic stochastic one, we show that it has a unique interior fixed point and examine the long-term trajectory behavior under specific conditions regarding the model parameters.

Code-switching between acronyms and their full forms within natural language
text is a common phenomenon, driven in part by the need to maintain a balanced
information-to-effort ratio. However, the widespread use of acronyms poses a
significance challenge to automated systems, given that abbreviations can lead to
ambiguous and misleading interpretations. This research aims to enhance the
performance of automated systems in detecting and obfuscating non-standard acronyms.
To this end, we propose AcroDetect, a neural system that leverages word embeddings
and context features to accurately identify acronyms within texts. Depending on the
available data, AcroDetect can be implemented using either a linear model or a deep
neural network. Our experimental results demonstrate that the AcroDetect-based
linear model outperforms existing acronyms detection systems, achieving a
parameter-efficient design while achieving robust performance in accent-based
English text. Furthermore, we introduce AcroDetect as an open-source tool, allowing
researchers to access and reproduce our results using the provided code, coupled
with pre-trained word embeddings for evaluation.

Quantum interference significantly affects charge transport properties, particularly in thermoelectric systems. By examining a quantum dot connected to two finite channels, it's evident that phase coherence can alter not only the magnitude but also the direction of the electric current. Furthermore, the addition of a magnetic field leads to the coexistence of multiple Minnler coefficients. The presence of channelinduced electric currents offers a potential method for detecting phase coherence times.

Our proposed DNA-storage system has unique features that set it apart from existing solutions. Its novel DNA-storage architecture enables efficient and easily updatable data organization, allowing for swift and space-effective metadata maintenance. This is achieved through the use of hierarchical indexing, which benefits from the inherent characteristics of DNA storage. Furthermore, we introduce the S.DNA system, our first complete end-to-end storage solution that integrates novel management, packaging, and mapping techniques. Our evaluation of the S.DNA system shows that it reduces write costs and access latencies while expanding the feasible storage capacity.

Topological insulators exhibit distinct characteristics of exceptional conductance and resistance.
Documents related to topological insulators, though numerous and intricate, necessitate thorough examination to be comprehended.
This study employs an advanced deep learning technique, namely, transformer-based language models, to classify the semantic properties of scientific documents.
The approach leverages the last 10 years of scientific literature on topological insulators to develop a sophisticated model capable of categorizing scientific documents into four distinct groups: abstract, introduction, body content, and conclusion.
The experiment yielded an outstanding accuracy rate of 90% for this classification task.
The study further explores the model's capacity to extract semantic information and uncover latent patterns within the dataset, showcasing its remarkable performance in this regard.

In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outgoing waves, which are crucial for synchronizing the entire system. Although these wave patterns are typically associated with chemical reactions, similar dynamics can also be observed in biological systems such as neuronal networks. This study focuses on a specific scenario characterized by localized areas with consistent internal dynamics, which generate traveling waves in a connected system, all outside of which has slower intrinsic frequencies. We investigate the properties of these wave patterns, particularly their speed and how they are influenced by the characteristics of the area that generates the waves and the surrounding system. Our analysis reveals that when synchronization occurs within this area, it gives rise to an infinite number of distinct pacemakers, each able to initiate waves in the system, with these different pacemakers being separated by spatial patterns of specific oscillation phases. Furthermore, this situation can lead to scenarios where different pacemakers compete when variations in the phase of oscillations within the synchronization region affect the frequency with which oscillations occur in that area.

A fundamental connection is drawn between quantum algorithms for estimating Shannon and von Neumann entropies and those for approximating the pure-state fidelity. This relationship enables the development of general methods for entropy estimation by applying fideline estimation techniques, such as feedback phase estimation, described in a recent preprint. As a result, two methods for calculating the asymptotic entropy estimation error are derived, highlighting that certain shadow tomography approaches based on fidelity estimation can be transformed into efficient estimators for entropy. One such technique achieves $\sqrt N$ accuracy with $O(P)$ queries per sample, where $N$ represents the number of drawn samples and $P$ is the preparation cost for $p$-mixtures. These findings result in a novel, efficient algorithm for estimating entropy from repeated measurements of prepared states, offering potential applications in areas like distribution learning and relative entropy estimation. The work also establishes a new, efficient method for calculating relative entropy that requires only a polynomial number of preparations and measurements, unlike a previously established lower bound of $N\sim p^2$. Lastly, some technical findings, such as a connection between Faithful State Vector Fidelity Estimation and the trace power, are presented, as well as a proof that finding a maximum-entropy state is a difficult task, which is proven NP-hard-reducible.

Implementing and deploying effective artificial intelligence (AI) solutions necessitates access to abundant datasets for the AI's comprehensive evaluation. Nevertheless, gathering these datasets can be cumbersome, requiring substantial time and resources to develop knowledge graphs or data catalogs. Even when such data is identified as suitable, ensuring its quality to reliably validate the AI's performance remains a major challenge. Ultimately, these technical hurdles can result in flawed AI models that fail to meet the high standards set by the "Garbage In, Garbage Out" principle. To develop robust AI systems, it is crucial to establish a data pipeline that integrates high-quality data with advanced analytics and machine learning algorithms. Fortunately, emerging big data processing frameworks facilitate this requirement. This paper presents a practical guide, leveraging Microsoft Power BI as a central tool for creating a data pipeline that meets this critical need. Power BI's capabilities in handling large datasets, coupled with its user-friendly interface, enable the efficient modeling and advanced computing. Specifically, we employ SQL within the Azure Synapse Analytics environment for extracting, transforming, and loading (ETL) operations, allowing for a swift and scalable data pipeline. Power BI is then used for the initial assessment of results, while DAX formulas are employed for complex computations that exceed SQL processing capabilities. To address data quality concerns, we implement methods such as Dynamic Data Masking within the ETL process and Power BI, alongside custom Data Quality Services (DQS) rule sets for more intricate validation. These examples illustrate a versatile and adaptable framework for

Physicians' written assessments and treatment suggestions in clinical text are linked to specific medical diagnoses through a process called ICD coding. Although CPT codes are used to determine physician reimbursement by reporting performed procedures,supplementary text areas in patient notes often contain crucial clinical information that can support decision-making. Text preceding or accompanying CPT code reporting is often utilized by hospital staff to ensure that reported procedures are justified. Although this information is not regularly captured, our study examines this valuable resource to predict the presence of clinical diagnosis codes in hospital discharge summaries, thereby demonstrating its potential use.

Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, along with illustrative examples.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in data has gained widespread importance. Currently, a lack of fully functional quantum computers has necessitated the use of classical supercomputers for training ML models. A recently developed approach allows the implementation of ML algorithms on quantum computers, leveraging the benefits of quantum mechanics to enhance data processing efficiency. The method involves the application of Hamiltonian learning, which can be executed on quantum computers. By treating the loss function as a Hamiltonian, its minimum corresponds to the desired weight configuration of the neural network. Although a quantum computer is not strictly required for the application of Hamiltonian learning, its access provides an alternative pathway for the evolution of quantum states and, consequently a different perspective on the optimization of NNs. A quantum simulator is used to conduct the necessary experiments, focusing on the implementation of the loss function and the testing of its effectiveness through various input configurations. The outcome shows that, while minimum losses can be found, the process does not correspond to an effective solution to the loss minimization problem. The minimum represent the scaled losses of the original loss function, which is acceptable for some applications but not others. The findings also highlight the significance of choosing an appropriate metric for the multi-class classification problem to ensure its applicability to quantum computers.

Our analysis encompasses all prime-field microlensing planets from the 2018 dataset provided by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder, incorporating 38 such objects in total. These planets were discovered through our manual examination of light curves and subsequent examination by other teams, all of which aligned in finding exactly 38 prime-field planets. Employing Bayesian analysis and comparing the results to four different galaxy models, our calculations indicate that roughly half of these planets reside within the Milky Way's disk, whereas the remaining half originated from objects located in front of other galaxies such as the Large Magellanic Cloud, the Small Magellanic Cloud, or the galaxy NGC 499. Furthermore, most of these prime-field planets exhibited a deviation in their behavior from that predicted by our four galaxy models, suggesting that further investigation into their distribution and densities within different galaxies is necessary to refine our understanding of their distribution across various galaxies.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based approaches and offer self-supervision for learning-based methods, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. Nonetheless, accurately replicating lighting conditions during the rendering process remains a pivotal challenge in developing effective differentiable image processing pipelines, given that incorrect light source parameters can lead to flawed gradients. This paper introduces a novel pipeline, called DiLight, that automatically determines unknown global illumination conditions from a single image, thereby enabling accurate light field reconstruction and generating reliable gradients for subsequent image reconstruction tasks. We evaluate the performance of DiLight within various different image processing pipeline scenarios, demonstrating its practical value in real-world applications.

Unpredictable traffic patterns are typically attributed to diverse routes and speed variations between them. Recent research has started to examine the impact of uncertainty in traffic estimation. This study builds on that work by introducing a new traffic uncertainty metric and a mechanism to estimate it. The proposed method breaks down total uncertainty into two distinct components - variability in traffic demand and variability in edge traversal times. Demand variability is calculated using a in real-time in real time (IRT) algorithm, while a 1-nearest neighbor time series forecasting is used. However, it's challenging to assign variability to individual edges without an complete understanding of the network, so a variational information flow based approach is developed to identify all possible paths in the network. Finally, path-level variability is used to allocate edge variability. Experimental results show that this approach effectively captures traffic uncertainty in a real network.

In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic and chaotic waves following a parameter adjustment. For weak nonlinearity in a network of N oscillators, a consistent theory based on a competition between phase diffusion and a frequency gap is developed to estimate the time scale for phase diffusion. For non-conservative systems, a similar but more intricate scenario arises and is especially intricate when the coupling is strong.

The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create spanning trees using random walks on a graph. Although these algorithms are popular for generating uniform spanning trees (USTs) in well-connected graphs with O(n log n) steps, their effectiveness suffers in graphs with poor connectivity or high diameter, as USTs usually include edges requiring many steps to traverse. To address this, a novel variant is proposed that generates a spanning tree using a self-avoiding random walk instead of a regular random walk. This variant, described and analyzed theoretically, demonstrates through simulations that the algorithm takes significantly fewer steps to generate a UST. An analysis of this variant's analysis through coupling reveals it converges to a uniform distribution over all possible USTs in terms of the maximum labeled node's position after just a constant number of steps, regardless of the graph's structure. This occurs because, due to the self-avoiding nature of the walks, nodes are integrated into the growing tree in a substantially different manner. Furthermore, a corresponding prefer-attachment variant is explored through simulations and theoretically analyzed.

This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset, comprising diverse multimedia elements such as audio, visual, and textual data, seamlessly integrated to facilitate complex musical tasks. The dataset features three categories of multi-modal entries: traditional sheet music accompanied by musical scores, real-world music performances accompanied by high-quality video footage, and lyrical content associated with musical scores. To capitalize on the multi-modal data, we introduce an innovative task called Multi-modal Musical Embedding (MME), which entails creating a unified representation by fusing information from sheet music, musical scores, video performance, and lyrics. This groundbreaking dataset and corresponding MME method pave the way for significant advancements in music research and pave the path for novel applications.

One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in this study with the Wikidata dataset. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration and querying of Linked Data entities. By utilizing distributional semantic models to identify and rank entity properties associated with user input in Ontodia, the method demonstrates improved results in enhancing user experience during visual data exploration.

We've discovered that in the nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation with variable refractive index and a defocusing cubic nonlinearity, dark solitons exhibit the same properties as in the standard model. However, a significant difference is that for a specific type of variable refractive index (power-law form), as intensity increases, dispersion also increases, which can lead to a new class of stable solitons with lower velocities. These stable solitons include those moving in one and two directions. Our findings also reveal that compact dark solitons are only possible when the refractive index variation is the same type as the soliton's intensity profile (power-law). Furthermore, we've observed that periodic dark solitons have a minimum velocity threshold.

This paper introduces the Co-AgVis project, a platform for researching and
developing visualization of analytics techniques that facilitate real-time
interaction between humans during analytical tasks. By leveraging VR/AR technology,
Co-AgVis innovates traditional Vis Analytics by enhancing spatial interaction
capacities. The project features a cloud-based metaverse where users can engage
with 3D visualizations through various interaction methods. Co-AgVis aims to fill a
gap in current Vis Analytics frameworks by providing a unified foundation for implementing
techniques focusing on human-machine collaboration in performing analytical tasks.

We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable symmetry, quasisymmetry, and 3D rotational invariance, thereby addressing a longstanding challenge in plasma confinement, particularly for near-axis ring optimization. By focusing on optimizing a relaxed version of quasisymmetry in the near-axis regime, we enable efficient stellarator designs that can be simulated and analyzed at bootstrapped equilibrium as a first step. To achieve this, we have created a hybrid of the relaxed toroidal symmetry and general $3D$ rotational invarvariant approaches that pushes quasisymmetry relaxed error to first order, thereby influencing relaxation and flux function relationships. This approach not only refines existing near-axis optimization but also paves the way for novel designs and offers a pathward direction for full-scale stellarator optimization.

In complex chemical systems, understanding and managing temperature variations in catalytic fixed bed reactors is crucial due to the inherent nonlinearity and sensitivity to initial conditions and temperature changes. Researchers have developed a feedback control strategy that uses localized temperature monitoring to maintain a desired steady-state temperature profile. By combining a one-dimensional heat transport model with a nonlinear heat generating function, which is perturbed by external disturbances, and designing a boundary heat flux controller in relation to measured temperature deviations, stable control is achieved. Notably, while the system's asymptotic behavior lacks traditional asymptotic independence from control parameters, researchers discovered that the controller's control parameter must solely depend on the control time parameter and not the transport parameter. Through both numerical simulations and a rigorous mathematical framework, including a H-inf optimal control analysis, the study validates the effectiveness of this control method.

Within eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, membraneless compartments arise through phase separation. Although this mechanism underpins the formation of these compartments, its precise molecular basis remains unclear. We present an abstractable model that elucidates how phase separation governs the time-dependent changes in concentration and free energy of macromolecular mixtures. Using this model, we demonstrate how varying interaction strengths and distances influences the emergence of phase separation, thereby explaining how these factors affect both static properties, such as low-frequency spectra and correlation lengths, and dynamic characteristics.

Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied how a major leading sunspot rotated in NOAA AR 11429 during two powerful solar flares. A notable sunspot rotated in an unconventional direction, influenced significantly by the solar eruptions. Moving disturbances within other sunspots, caused by the solar flares, traveled rapidly and altered the magnetic properties associated with the sunspots in question, providing valuable insights into the dynamic process governing the sunspots' development.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms a subset of oriented broken submersions introduced by Kreck and Zückert. The b-principle is a concept that z-equivariant map functions within the broader context of oriented broken submersions. The current note demonstrates the b-principle for b-map functions using the framework of oriented colored broken submersions, which can be found in the work by the author.

This study focuses on accelerating the solution of complex FEM-based cardiac mechanics problems through rigorous analysis of convergence rates for iterative solvers. The research delves into绥chekonsky's theorem, using it to evaluate the performance of two distinct preconditioners: the IL(0,0) and a task-specific variant named BP. The comparative analysis reveals that the task-specific algorithm outperforms the standard one in terms of convergence efficiency. The research further explores the effects of model parameter variations and boundary condition changes on solution patterns, as well as their impact on spectral properties. Notably, the IL(0,0) and BP preconditioners demonstrate similar efficiency across both small and large models, although BP's performance suffers with the introduction of new boundary conditions. A significant finding is that the spectrum of the preconditioned system remains relatively stable, indicating that solution patterns and boundary condition impacts on spectral properties can be reliably transferred between different models. This research also examines how parameter variations and boundary condition changes influence the condition number. The research reveals a substantial increase in condition number for both models under the IL(0,0) and BP preconditioners when electric parameters and a stiffening of the Cauchy stress model are applied, particularly for the BP preconditioner.

The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems supporting content creation, sharing, and management. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata pools and collaborative behavior. To unlock this potential, a comprehensive understanding of current systems is required, which involves characterizing these systems based on usage patterns, the evolution of user-generated content over time, and the underlying social dynamics.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has yet to be implemented with low-loss materials. This study presents the first experimental validation of sound wave control using non-reciprocal, bianisotropic metagratings. Acoustic logs demonstrate that a developed metamaterial with minimal loss enables efficient sound focusing at the design frequency, substantially outperforming standard diffraction limits. While some energy dissipation is observed, it is attributed to the specific design's inefficient long plexiglass pillars and can be further minimized with shorter structures. The achieved loss of 6 dB at 750 kHz is comparable to conventional p-wave transmitters. By exploring a simplified design with reduced construct complexity, this research verifies the practical feasibility of atherreciprocal acoustic metamaterials.

This paper primarily focuses on the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model. Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique, we demonstrate that the $L^2$ decay rate is given by $\ln^{-l}(e+t)$, with any positive integer $l$. Through the application of the time-weighted energy method, we manage to enhance this rate to $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Furthermore, we obtain precise $L^2$ estimates for the weighted norms, resulting in a eventual rate of $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{4}}$.

Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) through wireless connections offers a promising way to construct flexible and high-density networks. Uplink time division based scheduling (UL-TDS) has become a popular method for managing IAB links' quality, yet it poses challenges such as increased communication overhead and signal weakness for ul-SIG slots at lower IAB nodes. To tackle these challenges, UL-TDS with scheduling region selection (URS) has been proposed as a modern approach, allowing individual IAB nodes to choose their scheduling areas, but URS-IAB still relies on centralized control. To address this limitation, we devise a fully distributed scheduling region selection (DRRS) method, leveraging a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework where a shared communication protocol is presented, consisting of two phases: backhaul beacon management (BBM) and backhaul scanning and linking (BSL). Through cooperation and competition between nodes during the BBM phase, successful links are established in the BSL phase, with a reward structure that considers path length and node density. The results show that our proposed DRRS method significantly outperforms traditional UL-TDS and other comparative schemes.

In this study, we conduct an extensive examination of five leading global optimization algorithms as a hyperparameter configuration problem to understand the overall impact of their settings on performance. By utilizing three methods of sensitivity analysis and evaluating various adjustable parameters, such as covariance matrix adaptation, differential evolution, and non-dominated sorting, we analyze their effectiveness under different scenarios. Our primary focus concerns how setting choices affect performance and consistency when dealing with a broad range of test problems, covering numerous problem characteristics. Our results underscore the significant impact of adaptation options on performance and emphasize the need for further research into other essential setting choices, such as mutation frequency, population size, and starting set size. These findings offer valuable insights for problem solvers and contribute to a greater understanding of the importance of parameter tuning in solving complex optimization problems.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the waves they generate. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships are equivalent to a previously proposed atomic stability condition.

Despite significant advancements in reinforcement learning, many practical applications remain challenging due to the variable nature of real-world problems. Reinforcement learning models, which excel in controlled settings, often struggle with generalization beyond their initial problem. While supervisory learning solutions for generalization have been developed, the field of practical reinforcement learning experiences difficulties in achieving this. A novel framework is proposed to tackle real-world issues, which involves breaking down complex tasks into a collection of related and simple environments that can be considered individual Markov decision processes. A novel strategy for state representation, which is based on embedding technology, is developed to facilitate the sharing of common representations and policy components across these simplified tasks. Furthermore, a novel task embedding solution is presented to facilitate the transfer of task-specific knowledge to new, similar environments. A novel prioritized experience buffer is also developed to facilitate the efficient reuse of shared memories across similar environments. A novel framework for simultaneous learning of state and task embeddings is developed, which is grounded in a loss function that minimizes the differences between embedded representations of similar states or tasks while maximizing the distinctiveness of non-isomorphic states or tasks. A novel framework for phased learning is also implemented to facilitate phased learning of tasks and subsequent deployment to new, similar environments. A novel representation learning solution is developed to address real-world problems, which involves adapting the proposed state embedding approach and applying it to a collection of related tasks, which are simplified and unique Markov decision processes.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Monitor to expand its capabilities. By covering the L-band range from 1.0 to 2.4 microns, Liger will provide enhanced observational capabilities in these wavelengths. At 30 meters above the observatory, situated above most atmospheric interference, will enable virtually uninterrupted observation access to a variety of targets. Initially, Liger will operate via a video link to demonstrate its potential for all-sky monitoring, ultimately a tower-top instrument will be installed to automate continuous sky scans.

This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth traveling waves that arise in the context of 2D Euler equation dynamics, where the velocity fields exhibit sub-geometric decay in Fourier series. Notably, these waves cannot be categorized as equilibria in the Helmholtz-Kohlrasch equation, yet they demonstrate a form of stability under specific perturbations, exhibiting a form of amplitude stability.

We experimentally control the linear polarization of exciton-polariton condensates using optical traps with elliptical geometries that favor specific polarization modes. Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. These modes are selectively occupied by the condensate. Our results reveal a unique method for polarization control with potential applications in spin-based photonics and research on complex optical systems with adjustable coupling properties.

This study's primary objective is to provide evidence and disproofs for the deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equations including non-local gradient elements. The specific equations investigated fall within the following categories:

$\partial_t u=\nu \partial_x^2u+\lambda f(x,u)+\mu \partial_x g(x,u)\partial_yu+\partial_x h(x,u)\partial_y u,$

and

$\partial_t u=\nu \partial_x^2u+\lambda f(x,u)+\mu \partial_x g(x,u)\partial_y u+\partial_x h(x,u)\partial_y u+\rho \partial_x\partial_y\psi(x,u).$

Building upon the techniques for constructing probabilistic solutions developed in our previous research on the same subject,

Links to papers: https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01100,

we investigate the existence and non-existence of solutions to these equations within the space of continuous functions defined on the domain of $[0,1]\times[0,1]$. The considerations involve the equation's coefficients and initial conditions, specifically its spatial variation constant $C$, the function $\psi(x,u)$ that depends on the variational function $\psi(x)$, and the coefficients $\nu, \lambda, \mu, \rho$ that are non-negative and satisfy specific conditions.

The COVID-19 pandemic, originating in Wuhan, China, has swiftly spread across the globe, with the World Health Organization officially designating it as a global health emergency in March 2020. In response to this unprecedented situation, governments have implemented stringent measures such as isolation, hygiene precautions, and frequent handwashing to curb the virus's transmission. As a result, these measures have primarily influenced developing nations, where the government in each individual case assesses its own requirements. The most effective course of action to contain the virus in any given nation is to enforce frequent handwashing and limit gatherings. To provide a clear understanding of these actions, we present a multi-agent reinforcement learning simulation that can effectively mitigate the spread of an infectious agent within a population by enforcing a common frequency of interaction limit among selected groups. By representing each individual as a rational agent that chooses the optimal admissible interaction frequency with other agents to optimize its objective function, we find that the frequency of interaction limit serves as a common language of social distancing, capable of limiting the spread of infectious agents and reducing peak epidemics to manageable levels.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, each of size k from the integers, share a sumset with a relatively small cardinality (less than or equal to 3k-4), then their elements can be organized in a non-decreasing sequence that shares a common difference. Our aim is to refine this conclusion when A equals B in the original hypothesis. Achieving this goal requires a broader understanding that if subsets A and B have a sumset with a particularly compact size (at most 2.5k), their elements can be arranged as part of an arithmetic progression, with a potentially looser bound of 2.6k while allowing distinct subsets A and B.

Medical reports and imaging are crucial medical tools that aid in diagnosis and treatment planning. To enhance the precision of specific medical tasks, combining radiological and pathological information can contribute to more effective disease diagnosis and treatment. This study introduces a novel framework for multi-modal cancer diagnosis and severity assessment, specifically针对 lung cancer. The primary goal is to leverage a language model to extract valuable information from radiological reports and integrate it with pathological data, such as tumor size and location derived from CT scans. The proposed framework employs a hierarchical attention score calculation between report segments and side information, enabling effective utilization of both. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework achieves superior results in several lung cancer-related tasks compared to using report data alone. Notably, it showcases excellent performance in cancer severity assessment, an area previously unexplored with only radiological data. The proposed framework provides a unique approach for exploring the integration of report-based and imaging-related information for semantic medical image enhancement in vision and language tasks.

X-ray images are easily accessible, cost-effective and quick to obtain, and thus, crucial for early detection of severe COVID-19 symptoms such as acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. As a contribution, we present severe COVID-19 feature point detectors that leverage the inherent semantic characteristics of X-ray images, and utilize a pixel-wise detector model based on Convolutional Neural Networks. By exploiting the interplay between these semantic features and lung regions, we demonstrate the potential of our approach in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure prognosis. Furthermore, through experiments on the publicly available IIFA dataset, we achieve an average prediction accuracy of 68%, surpassing the performance of current methods by a notable margin.

We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem involving an $L^2$-normalized eigenfunction and an associated eigenvalue. As the associated frequency tends to infinity, we investigate the behavior of the eigenfunction's L2-norm. Through numerical computations and one dimensional proof we demonstrate that the energy associated with the transmission eigenfunctions unbounded and that they are
unconditionally oscillatory in all directions. These findings hold for radially symmetric media where the refractive index is real, bounded, and piecewise $H^1(\Omega)$-smooth.

To expand a dialogue system's capabilities, it's crucial to detect and categorize user intents that were not initially part of the system. Existing methods for new intent discovery focus on identifying which classes an unlabeled user input may belong to. However, there has been limited progress in actually incorporating new intents into the system once they are discovered. We aim to bridge this gap by investigating how to integrate new intents for accurate intent classification of subsequent user inputs. Our proposed solution involves training a joint model that learns both user input representation and the parameters of a latent intent space, optimizing it through a contrastive loss function. This model enables efficient integration of new intents with minimal retraining. We evaluate our method using a large-scale, real-world hotel booking dataset and observe significant improvements over baseline models, with an area under the precision recall curve (AUPR) area difference of 0.1310 and a BLEU score difference of 0.3214. The code for our model is publicly available on GitHub.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.
In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups.

This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. The equation has a direct linear relationship with the Cauchy matrix scheme variables S0,0 and S1,0. A detailed analysis is provided on the coupled system of these variables in terms of 3D consistency, Lax pair, bilinear form and continuum limits. The study employs adelic theory with both a 4th order lattice KdV and a 2nd lattice KdV.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship representation method causes object features to dominate the expression of relationship embeddings, impairing the ability of VRD models to accurately detect semantically similar relationships. Furthermore, our study introduces RelFormer, a novel visual relationship detection model that leverages a query-based approach. RelFormer employs a decoder transformer to learn rich, representative relationship representations and accurately detect various relationships. RelFormer also enhances model interpretability by allowing the identification of influential visual regions for relationship detection. With the RelFormer, we achieved superior performance, including 68.6 mAP on the COCO dataset and 72.4 mAP on the VCD dataset, setting new state-of-the-art records.

A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the quantum correlation cost is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord by a factor related to trace-norm squared. Furthermore, the quantum correlation cost can be utilized in calculating Bures quantum work and is applicable to weakly mixed states. In contrast to other correlation costs, this new measure exhibits certain advantageous characteristics in practical applications.

Understanding social environments in images is a complex process that requires social knowledge. Currently, most knowledge bases for social purposes are based on general social environments, which differ from the characteristics of visual scenes. This paper introduces a social relationship graph that captures fundamental elements of visual social environments, allowing for insights into social interactions. A graph-based neural network is proposed to infer social relationships between objects, and this model is paired with a new benchmark for social relationship recognition. The dataset, 3DGlyph, consists of 3D indoor environments with social relationships between 3D objects, and when combined with an indoor scene dataset, RealWorldGlyph, demonstrates that the model achieves high accuracy in social relationship recognition, matching state-of-the-art performance.

Graph Neural Networks are increasingly being used in computer vision, but they often struggle with efficiency, as dense graph network models result in excessive computation and memory usage. Furthermore, many graph neural network models are limited to static structures, making them inadequate for handling dynamic vision problems. To address these issues, we developed a new approach called Dynamic Graph Message Passing Network, which efficiently models long-range dependencies. Our proposed method also integrates a dynamic attention mechanism that selectively filters out irrelevant pixels, and a novel graph pooling technique that manages the growth of the graph structure. Our experiments demonstrate that, in contrast to conventional graph neural networks, our approach outperforms them on multiple large-scale datasets.

Optimizing embedded system multiplications often involves techniques like shifting and adding (shift-and-add, SAA), but can be time-consuming due to the large number of operations required. One approach is to use modular compacting (MC) to represent any number using negative base representations. This has been utilized in various negative radix systems, but each has its own set of advantages. This research explores designing an efficient embedded multiplier based on MC in radix -2 and explores the use of bit-parallel multiplication in radix -2 for reduced complexity. Furthermore, it proposes a variable-length compacting algorithm and a bit-parallel multiplication method in radix -2 without carry propagation, resulting in a reduced number of bits needed for the partial products. This leads to a lower hardware requirement and makes the design suitable for use in a wide range of embedded systems.

The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has recently given rise to a growing research field, known as quantum deep learning. Despite previously being separate entities, advancements have revealed that quantum circuits share parallels with artificial neural networks, paving the way for widespread adoption. This paper delves into the foundational aspects and core principles of quantum deep learning, highlighting key breakthroughs along the way. It also explores the challenges inherent in quantum deep learning research from multiple viewpoints, followed by a discussion of prospective future directions and practical applications.

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator technology continues to play a crucial role in high-energy particle physics experiments, influencing both upgraded existing facilities and new facility developments. Recent RF technology advancements have opened up possibilities for exploring future particle physics experiments. This paper presents an advanced power coupling system developed by SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory and collaborating institutions, which can handle the transmission of high power (up to 500 kW) at 1.3 GHz with high efficiency while minimizing heat generation. This system has successfully undergone testing, demonstrating its capability to couple high power with high efficiency and distribute it evenly to accelerator cavities.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using relativistic hydrodynamics to analyze the data from heavy-ion collisions.

Our analysis assesses the feasibility of detecting primordial black holes via their Hawking radiation, making RFI detections a novel detection method. We have provided an accurate calculation of the R brightness temperature caused by such black hole evaporation, making several key discoveries in the process. Firstly, we determined the Hawking radiation-induced brightness temperature to be approximately 3.25 times 10^16 Kelvin, assuming a universe composed entirely of evaporating PBHs. We further found that the radiation's power flux and PBH mass are directly proportional, and the peak temperature and mass of evaporating PBHs may coincide with various RF frequencies, depending on the selected sensitivity threshold. We also highlighted the role of Hawking radiation as a significant background noise source for upcoming radio telescopes, providing essential guidance for future observations. We emphasize that our research outcomes can be reliably applied to various radio observatories, including the FAST and SKA, due to their elevated ground-up viewing angles and restricted horizontal viewing fields.

Integrating Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) into cloud services allows users to securely outsource data processing tasks without exposing their encrypted information to the service provider. The cloud provider can perform computations on encrypted data, returning a ciphertext that, when decrypted by the user, yields the correct plaintext result - this property is known as functional confidentiality. The current state-of-the-art approach to achieving this property involves Shamir's secret sharing and secure multiplication techniques, which however incurs a performance cost. This paper presents an enhanced secret sharing scheme that significantly reduces noise in HE ciphertexts after a computation, thereby improving efficiency and enabling faster retrieval of results. The technique combines public and private sharing schemes, taking advantage of the public domain to reduce noise without unnecessarily increasing noise. The performance improvements achieved include a fourfold increase in speed for secret sharing, up to tenfold efficiency gains in multi-party computations, and up to fiftyfold efficiency improvement in FHE-based Outsource Data Analysis.

Researchers have developed a constant-factor, polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for a broad category of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). This PTAS applies to CSPs with uniform constraints, each allowing a limited number of inputs and a symmetrical cost function. This scheme outperforms the previously established $O(1)$-factor PTAS. The new approximation scheme is based on a reduction from CSPs to codeword discovery problems on distributions that can then be rapidly sampled due to its symmetry property. The sample size required is inversely proportional to the fault rate and thus may be significantly larger than what is needed for supported problems. The reduced sample complexity is achieved by shifting the domain from exact discovery in the noise to partial symbolic string (PSS) exact discovery. The shift in CSP formulation involves reformulating CSPs as discovery in the noise of a distributed cost version of CSPs. The discovery runtime for a domain of size $N$ is $O(N/\epsilon)$ and this leads to an efficient algorithm that is sensitive to the inverse of the domain size. The proposed PTAS is applicable to a broad category of CSPs that can accommodate any constraint size. The time complexity for this new PTAS is specifically $T(N) \cdot \log^{O(1)}_2(N/\epsilon)$, where $T(N)$ is an upper bound on the cost function for inputs of size $N$. Pre-trained language models possess the capability to learn syntactic structures, and when combined with language-specific parsing methods, they can achieve high parsing accuracy. This research investigated the extent to which specific elements within the transformer architecture contribute to this capability. By examining the effects of modifying the weights of the self-attention mechanism, particularly those associated with linear projection matrices used for queries and keys, we found that such modifications significantly influence the syntactic parsing accuracy. Notably, increasing the weight of the residual connection in these specific matrices resulted in consistent improvements in parsing accuracy across multiple datasets. Building on this understanding, we developed a new syntactic parsing method called Syntactic Augmentation, which utilizes such changes to pre-trained language models to enhance parsing accuracy effectively.

High-definition hyperspectral images possess the capacity to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate scenes by analyzing their spectral patterns. This capability has led to their adoption in various computer vision challenges, including the fundamental task of semantic segmentation. This study presents a novel approach, Hyperspectral Region-aware Transformer (H-Ranformer), to tackle the semantic segmentation challenge in an urban environment based on the HSI XSens LHS. The H-Ranformer addresses the limited local context awareness and insufficient high-level context integration in existing segmenters by introducing a specific architecture. This includes a region-aware hyperpatch embedding layer to enhance local context awareness and an alternating hypernode and hyperpatch attention mechanism to overcome the challenge of insufficient high-level context integration. The proposed method's effectiveness and distinct advantages are demonstrated through comprehensive experiments and additional analyses.

This study reveals evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation after leaving the main sequence due to their angular momentum. As a result, they should exhibit rapid rotation at their core. Contrary to expectations, rotational oscillations in the star called the $\nu$ Doradus show a significantly slower core rotation, about 1.5 times the surface rotation, or 330.0454 days, when first detected in 2015. From 2015 to 2020, a project involving the $\nu$ Doradus star revealed a particularly striking internal rotation pattern. Using a unique technique that applies the concept of helioseismology to astroseismology, researchers found that the star's core and its outer layers are rotating at significantly different rates. Additionally, scientists noticed an external layer of the star that rotates more slowly than both the core and the surface, located approximately 7.5 stellar radii below the surface. As the star continues to evolve into a giant, its internal and external components with distinct rotation rates may lead to tangential velocity differences of up to 30 km s-1 between them. This could potentially cause the development of differential rotation within the ectosphere.
