Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an additional regulator involving π. This leads to a complete resolution of the denominator for all basis elements of weighted multiple zeta value spaces related to even central binomial series at weights up to 20, integrating Apéry-type terms as required.

Following a recent discovery in 2017 of a potential Y dwarf with a temperature as low as 1200K, a necessary step is to verify its low temperature through its indistinguishable colors in the NIR range from those of typical brown dwarfs at lower temperatures. A new set of filters was designed to accomplish this, specifically filters YJHsW, with the former intended to examine a low-temperature object and the latter checking for any saturation of these objects' light curves. We carried out observations with the Magellan-MIKE telescope on MIKE-2016-04-1 on LU20170101W01 LHS 258b, with its initial goal of ruling out a low-temperature object being met by establishing YJHsW color ranges to differentiate a Y dwarf from typical brown dwarfs at lower temperatures. With the help of MIKE telescope's data collection capabilities of a high frame rate and low resolution spectrum settings on the star, we were able to verify a low-temperature object's color pattern consistency on an exposed star, with the aid of a high frame rate capability of a low resolution spectrum settings on a high-temperature object at J2000 16h24m21.65+39 0704.66, we were able to verify a low-temperature object's color pattern consistency on an exposed star, with

The ALICE Collaboration has found that in high-energy proton-proton and proton-lead collisions, there is a positive correlation between radial flow and either charged-particle multiplicity per unit of rapidity or transverse momentum scale in lead-lead collisions. This observation suggests that radial flow increases as the density of charged particles decreases. In line with predictions from hydrodynamics at low viscosity, the data also indicates regular flow patterns across different charged-particle densities, allowing for a detailed examination of how radial flow responds to variations in the system's energy scale. Notably, the average transverse momentum of charged-particle pairs S_{<p_T<T_ave>}} exhibits increased sensitivity to charged-particle density for values of T_ave below 2 GeV, compared to all-p_T charged-pairs <p_T>. This result points to a significant role played by high-flow particles at lower values of T_ave, offering valuable insight into the dynamics of the QCD system created during high-energy collisions.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme. The proposed approach can be applied liberally and may contribute to reduced DPD uncertainty in the future.

Particulate materials from the Moon and Mars can be sintered together at relatively low temperatures to form a solid mass.  By subjecting simulated Martian and Lunar soil samples to cold water up to 700 °C, researchers observed that the materials develop a porous structure with significant porosity levels.  The samples were then compressed to assess their mechanical properties, and their microstructures were analyzed.  Additional studies involved scanning electron microscopy to examine the samples at a fine level, as well as X-ray microtomography scanning for 3D imaging of their internal structures.  The results suggest that the materials develop a complex network of bonds between particles.  Specifically, sample ML-7 treated at 400 °C exhibited exceptional bond density with minimal pore sizes, and this material exhibited a compressive strength exceeding 1 MPa.  Martian sample MS-5 performed similarly to Lunar samples at temperatures above 500 °C, exhibiting sufficient mechanical properties for in-place construction at 500-600 °C.  Microscopic analysis revealed that both materials consist of distinct bond types, and tomography scans disclosed that both materials consist of distinct bond types, and that both materials consist of distinct bond types, and that both materials consist of distinct bond types.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This study examines the effect of liquid-solid slip, intermediate between no-slip and free slip conditions, on the growth rate of perturbations in a liquid film. For intermediate slip conditions, certain properties of the two extremes are maintained while other characteristics are altered in both steady and time-dependent scenarios.

By comparing the $H\alpha$ and Brackett-$\beta$ emission rates of 31 galaxies from a previous study, we determined that star formation rates calculated using $H\alpha$ are overestimated due to $H\alpha$ photon losses, which are not fully compensated for increased gas temperatures in certain conditions. Consequently, temperature-dependent star formation rates would be required for accurate measurements in such cases. Our analysis also revealed that star formation rates calculated using $H\alpha$ are significantly affected by dust opacity, even in galaxies with low dust-to gas mass ratios. We found that employing a single, fixed value for scattering efficiency is insufficient for accurately measuring $H\alpha$ photon losses and, subsequently, determining star formation rates. Furthermore, we observed that galaxies with higher ionization parameter values exhibit greater discrepancies between $H\alpha$ and recombination line-based star formation rate measurements. We also compared our results to a previous study, which found similar outcomes in star-forming galaxies with low dust opacity and high gas temperatures. Our analyses combined theoretical calculations of recombination, dust opacity, and photon escape, as well as empirical data from a large sample of galaxies, highlighting the necessity for incorporating accurate physical models of dust opacity and photon escape into future dust models.

This paper completes the classification of braided auto-equivalences of local modules over spin-tube categories associated with orbifolds, given a fixed genus. These auto-equivalences can be represented as the group $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ for generic tori, six specific orbifolds related to the $A_{k-1}$ series, and four exceptional cases. Furthermore, we identify ten possible orbifolds that generate the exceptional orbifolds through the generators of the generators of the orbifolds.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread and by Petersen and Collins for species migration. Its continuous analogue was developed by Fisher with a solution now known as the Fisher-KPP equation. Researchers have successfully adapted it for discrete lattices resulting in the Fisher-KPP master equation. Researchers found that when the lattice spacing was reduced, it could be mapped onto the continuous Fisher-KPP equation. However, this mapping was only partially successful as some terms were not accounted for in the approximation. As a result, a new correction term was identified which arises due to fluctuation effects typical of systems at the mesoscopic scale. This correction manifests as an additional diffusion term in the Lindblad equation analogous to the Fisher-KPP equation.

This task involves identifying individual handwritten mathematical terms and classifying them into specific categories, focusing on handwritten mathematical expressions. A significant portion of modern education is conducted through writing, making the hand a primary tool for learning and communication. However, the inability to interpret handwritten mathematical expressions in the same way as printed text is a significant barrier in both education and computer science. To address this challenge, a initial step towards the broader goal of handwritten mathematical expression recognition is needed. In this study, a significant dataset of handwritten mathematical symbols, operators, and delimiters is introduced, collected from 30 various writing instruments, representing a diverse range of handwriting styles. A robust deep learning-based classifier is developed, achieving high accuracy on in-domain writing styles at 99.54% and generalizing well to unseen writing instruments, with a generalization performance of 97.86%. The proposed solution demonstrates promising potential for the ultimate goal of handwritten mathematical expression recognition.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach leverages a learned nonparametric distribution with median and dispersion parameters. The former is used as a phony transition probability for speech generation, while the latter serves as a dummy speech flow value. Crucially, this method employs an iterative reweighted least squares solver for solving a complex nonparametric distribution learning problem under a missing data framework. Evaluation results from the TTS-E evaluation package demonstrate a significant improvement of around 17% in median duration accuracy for Chinese, resulting in more natural synthesized speech due to decreased articulation anomalies. Furthermore, the proposed method has minimal computational requirements, allowing for online learning and efficient synthesis with precomputed hidden states.

Species distribution is often evaluated using various spatial metrics.  This research focuses on the statistical inference of ecological indices, where models are developed. It examines how distribution is estimated, considering the impact of sampling design and the detection of species. Examples from Belgian forest habitats illustrate the findings. Further research is required to refine estimation methods, particularly for diverse habitat types and species assemblages. This study can be applied to various detection methods, including visual species surveys.

Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to algorithm-supported diagnostics. TheSkinHelper was created to overcome these obstacles by providing an AI-driven diagnostic tool for malignant skin images, developed in cooperation with scientists and doctors specializing in skin diseases. To enhance the diagnostic process, we developed an interactive deep learning approach that aids the doctor in the diagnostic decision-making process. The Hinge Loss supported Spatial Attention mechanism ( HMSA) improves the original Batch Normalization supported Spatial Attention mechanism (N SMA) approach by forcing the neural network to concentrate on the most important regions in a picture by making it distinguish between relevant and irrelevant focus areas. The results indicate that our deep learning approach outperformed state-of-the-art diagnostics and improved diagnostic confidence by 10%. A usability study showed that doctors preferred using our system over traditional methods and felt more confident in their diagnoses. TheSkinHelper offers new possibilities to support skin cancer diagnosis and treatment decision-making, ultimately enhancing patient care.

To capture the complex nature of type Ia supernovae spectral data, a physics-based probabilistic autoencoder using the Flame code is proposed. This neurosimulator takes in a supervised neural network's results for the same supernovae model and trains on their temporal spectra and associated kinetic parameters. By employing an encoder-decoder structure, the model discovers and compresses key patterns in spectral data that can then reconstruct supernovae spectra and dynamics with varying levels of noise. Furthermore, by applying the variational inference technique, statistical distributions for target parameters are estimated through a regressive neural network. It is demonstrated that S/AVE discovers the underlying solar opacity-driven spectral variations and produces accurate predictions for kinetic parameters, showcasing its potential for analyzing spectral data and generating supernovae samples with specified dynamics.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a dusty galaxy. The outflow, linked to a bright [OIII] emission line, has been studied using ALMA and HST. The data suggests an extensive outflow extending over 15,000 light-years and with an extensive size of over 15,000 light-years. The mass of the outflow is approximately 10 million solar masses. The outflow velocity at the center of the galaxy is around 400 km/s. The most likely explanation for the outflow is a central starburst or active galactic nucleus. However, other explanations like galaxy interactions or tidal forces are also possible.

In a laboratory setting, researchers studied the interaction between an upward flow of warm water and the entrainment of suspended particles at the plume's leading edge. By combining high-speed cameras with Particle Image Velocimetry, they mapped the flow field, including the distribution of particles. Comparing the flow with and without the effect of the entrained particles, they found the presence of particles significantly altered the flow dynamics, reducing the region of turbulence by over 50%. When particles with a higher density than the fluid and a moderate buoyancy were allowed to settle, they were observed to accumulate at the plume's periphery where the fluid's momentum is lower. As a result, the plume's growth in the radial direction was restricted due to increased particle concentration and decreased turbulence. Due to decreased turbulence and increased viscosity, the vertical growth of the plume in the direction of the fluid flow was increased. Due to increased fluid viscosity, fluid mixing was decreased and reduced to the periphery of the plume. These observations suggest that the growth of turbulent plumes can be distinguished based on the direction of fluid flow and particle suspension.

Modeling disease spread on complex networks, such as contact graphs built from various types of node interactions, has been a prevalent approach. This paper considers networks constructed from nodes in close proximity and their relationships, formed by edges, as hyperedges connecting multiple nodes. These hyperedges enable a more precise representation of disease transmission between groups of individuals, thus facilitating a more accurate modeling of virus spread. We examine the virus propagation in such networks by applying the Susceptible-Infected model and analyzing the expected number of infected nodes. To manage the computational complexity, we devise an efficient randomization technique that enables a precise prediction of infected node counts without simulating the entire process. This method also reveals a previously unknown connection between virus propagation and influence propagation in networks. Finally, through experimentation on synthetic networks and real-world data, we demonstrate that considering nodes within the same group as a cluster allows for a more accurate prediction of virus spread than treating each node separately.

Recently, extensive studies have been conducted on two-dimensional (2D) magnetic semiconductors, particularly with a focus on CrI$_3$. This specific material exhibits unique properties stemming from its exchange interaction, resulting in a highly controllable exchange field via an external magnetic field. What's more, its thin-film version displays an interesting phenomenon where spin orientation changes in response to external magnetic fields, influenced by its lattice anisotropy. To better comprehend this behavior, our theoretical analysis has investigated Landau levels in 2D CrI$_3$ by taking into account both its exchange field and anisotropic effective mass. Our findings indicate that adjusting the external magnetic field allows for the manipulation of the Landau level spacing, yielding various spectral patterns. Additionally, our numerical simulations have shown that the Landau level absorption spectrum of CrI$_3$ is influenced by its anisotropic effective mass and valley-dependent band structure, resulting in distinguishable valley-dependent absorption peaks that could be utilized for detecting valley polarization.

Researchers have observed solar-type stars exhibiting rotation patterns that initially increase towards the stellar core, but then shift to a decreasing rotation towards the core in stars with weaker magnetic fields. The role of the Rossby number in influencing stellar differential rotation has been investigated through three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations of convective stars of various masses. These simulations revealed an inverse relationship between the Rossby number and the star's angular velocity variation for those with high convective speeds, however for stars with lower convective speeds, the differences in rotation within the convective layer gradually diminish as the Rossby number rises. The magnetic fields generated by the simulated dynamo processes are primarily concentrated in the equatorial regions of the stars. The magnetic fields also have a significant impact on the position of the convective boundary, raising it above the levels predicted by previous mean-field magnetohydrodynamic models.

Deep multimodal learning through combination of inputs has long been a challenge, 
with existing models typically requiring a separate embedding layer for each modality.
This causes difficulties in learning the fusion when distinct inputs are involved, 
especially if one mode is significantly weaker than others. To address this, we propose 
the K-fan deep model for handling multiple inputs in a self-supervised pre-training and 
self-supervised contrastive pre-training framework. By allowing each modality to 
share a single shared-layer K-fan deep model, it facilitates learning through 
contrast. We also describe a novel method for embedding graph data, essential for 
multimodal image-graph applications. We evaluate our model in two real-world 
scenarios, the MS-COCO description grounding and the S3DIS place recognition 
tasks, achieving superior results in both scenarios. The source code for our model is 
available at https://github.com/ashwinjha98/KFM.

The use of model checking as a method for verifying the correctness of concurrent programs has been demonstrated. However, its feasibility, particularly when dealing with programs that perform model checking in their own runtime, remains an unresolved issue. We have developed an approach for verifying the concurrent execution of the model checking algorithm within a Seesat verification environment, successfully applying it to verify the correct parallel processing of a Seesat model for the Stop-and-Wait protocol. Our multi-threaded Seesat models are designed without any pre-defined assumptions about execution order, and we have established both a formal and informal argument for their accuracy in representing the stop-and-wait algorithm. We have also provided an implementation of our multi-threaded model in the C programming language and an accompanying formal model in ProVerbes for verifying the stop-and-wait properties of our C implementation. Our approach, although not yet fully automated, is relatively straightforward to apply to other models and programs, although it does involve some adjustments to execution models to add thread management structures.

In the context of active misinformation dissemination, fact-checking initiatives are gaining prominence. Although fact-checks are publicly available, understanding their effectiveness in closing the information gap remains unclear, particularly considering the closed nature of WhatsApp for limiting misinformation spread. This research investigates the impact of fact-checks shared on WhatsApp by examining its closed environment. By combining data from Facebook and WhatsApp in Mexico, our analysis reveals the closed structure of WhatsApp groups limits misinformation sharing but does not prevent the spread of fact-checks and high-quality information.

We analyze a branching population where each individual's offspring distribution depends on the population's frequency spectrum. A frequency spectrum consists of unique trait types and their corresponding relative frequencies. Assuming continuous trait space and continuous relative frequencies, we obtain a branching population model with a mean measure that evolves according to a system of integro-differential equations. This model can be approximated by discrete-type distributions, which converge as the number of discretization points increases.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. This AReLU incorporates two key characteristics that align with our system's objectives: selective feature emphasis and non-linearity. By incorporating these factors, the AReLU enables our system to concentrate on the most relevant aspects of spoken data and effectively differentiate between genuine and fabricated voices. Experimental evaluations using the Voice Conversion and DAS-Spooner datasets demonstrate the substantial performance gains of the AReLU over conventional, non-linearity and selective emphasis features, as well as a standard linear baseline.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model, naturally incorporates inflationary scenarios through its coupling with superfields, making it an attractive framework for theoretical physicists. However, the same features, including the K\"ahler potential, pose a problem as they can cause issues with the stability of particles referred to as scalars, leading to scenarios known as the "polony problem." Despite these challenges, researchers have found a solution by modifying the models with a specific type of polynomic K\"ahler potential, effectively mitigating the scalars' instability and aligning their masses with observational data from the Planck experiment, particularly in situations where the inflaton field is close to zero planck. To further substantiate their models, the authors also investigated the renormalization effects of their models involving the field of inflation.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate light based on its propagation direction, whereas systems based on photon pair correlations exhibit unique nonreciprocal characteristics. In this study, a new phenomenon is discovered where the correlation between photons changes when they propagate in opposite directions. This change is observed in the cross-spectral correlation function between the photons' spectrum and spatial distribution, and it's demonstrated without the need for special spectral filters.

In order to achieve practical large-scale quantum computers, it is crucial to address material flaws in superconducting quantum circuits that cause decoherence. This thesis develops quantum design rules for applying quantum design principles to engineering, with a focus on improving quantum hardware reliability. The research achieved the following outcomes: a) a novel design principle was discovered - the principle of quantum impedance matching, explaining how to match the interfaces between quantum hardware components for optimal performance, thereby enabling seamless integration of different quantum system components; b) a se-metrology device was created - a segmented electrical transmission line with known dimensions, serving as a quantum-standard ruler to measure the se-metre; and c - the principle of se-metrology was implemented, demonstrating its utility in transmission line debugging while providing an exact calculation of the se-metre.

We are looking for infinite cardinals $\kappa$ that allow for a division of the real number line $\mathbb{R}$ into $\kappa$ unique Borel sets. The well-known Hausdorff solution indicates that such a division is possible for $\aleph_1$. However, the main conclusion of this note is the establishment of an interesting theorem stating that for a wide variety of scenarios, the number in the Hausdorff solution happens to be the smallest possible $\kappa$ that surpasses or equals the cardinality of the real numbers and the number of uncountable regressive functions on $\omega_1$. The given information also includes references to prior research that show that a specific hypothesis allows for a division be possible for $\aleph_1<\kappa$. The above mentioned research can be found in the following sources: P. Komj\'{a}th and P. Unger, 'A different order type of subsets of Borel sets', Publications of the Research Institute for Mathematical Sciences, 37 (2002), no. 8, 1343-1362; S. Shelah, 'Proper and improper forcing', in: Proper and improper forcing, 2nd Edition, Springer Monographs in Mathematics. Springer, New York, 2004; B. Zaidenberg 'One-to-many automorphisms of countable structures via C2-forcing', arX

In the 1970s and 1980s, commodity trading advisors (CTAs) led the alternative investment space, but their seemingly modest cAve of returns failed to attract investors in today's market. Historical C4 data from cAves between 1985-2019, coupled with CTA strategy information, led to a迥然 divergent discovery. Specifically, C4s of CTA-managed funds tended to exhibit positive short-term reversal, in stark contrast to the negative short-term reversal typically observed in mean-reverting CTA funds, which are typically devoid of short-term reversal. Subsequent out-of-sample testing confirmed that short-term reversal traders were able to profit from both CTA-absent and CTA-present funds during both bull and bear markets. Notably, short-term reversal profits from CTA-absent funds were notably higher than their non-CTA counterparts. These results suggest that the presence of short-term reversal traders distorted the cAve performance of CTA-managed funds, thereby masking their genuine risk-adjusted returns.

Identifying the application protocol is a crucial step in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate process for real-time data analysis. Although determining the application protocol from raw packet information appears straightforward, it becomes a complex and computationally intensive task due to the variety of protocols and their constantly evolving characteristics. Although current approaches rely on machine learning techniques, there is a pressing need to enhance their解释ability due to their lack of transparency in decision-making processes, which hinders effective security decisions. To address this issue, we developed a novel approach based on extended decision tables (EDT) for a more interpretable classification method. By training an EDT model once, it can perform classification and provide clear human-readable justifications. Our results demonstrate that the accuracy of the EDT model surpasses other deep learning-based methods, such as ResNet, while significantly improving the clarity of its decision-making process.

Electrostatic gating allows for controlling the population of particles in degenerate quantum systems, enabling the comparison of thermal, thermal-assisted, and non-thermal mechanisms. This study demonstrates the ability to manipulate magnons in a Yttrium-Indium Ferriate spin wave device through electrostatic gating, revealing that these magnons can serve as reliable and controllable information transporters. The findings indicate that magnons can be fully depleted via electrostatic gating, making them suitable candidates for integrating into semiconductor devices and developing novel forms of quantum computation.

A novel approach to federated learning addresses the issue of non-identically distributed data across devices by creating a virtual server that aggregates client parameters without observing local data. This innovative method employs two crucial components, the Parameter Injection Module and the Parameter Aggregation Module, both utilizing neural networks and attention mechanisms to enhance model performance and generalizability on non-identically distributed data. As a control mechanism, the module evaluates model effects on global accuracy and provides insights for subsequent model adjustments. Through comprehensive evaluations on diverse neural network architectures and data sets, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance and generalizability in comparison to conventional federated averaging.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both hyperentanglement of photons and the quantum Fourier transform are employed. The proposed solution will serve as a useful resource for developing high-dimensional quantum computation and communication.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink channel estimation in multi-user systems that leverage intelligent-reflecting-surface (IRS) technology without employing a maximum ratio-combining receiver. The paper begins with a detailed analysis of the structured nonlinearity inherent in the uplink received signals generated by the IRS. Building on this understanding, a novel post-processing method for estimating the channel has been developed within a compressed-sensing framework. The performance of this novel estimator is extensively evaluated. Notably, this framework exhibits considerable non-linear characteristics, which significantly impacts the complexity of traditional maximum likelihood channel estimation techniques. In contrast, the proposed estimator demonstrates a substantial reduction in computational complexity. The research findings indicate that, in scenarios characterized by high user counts and reflective surface area, and when utilizing maximum ratio-combining, a considerable savings in channel estimation bandwidth can be achieved.

This study explores various characteristics of public discourse in U.S. news coverage concerning COVID-19, covering topics like death counts, personal stories, and information on vaccines, from January 2020 to July 2021. Utilizing a large dataset of local, online, and national news articles, as well as advanced natural language processing techniques, we examine how different types of coverage evolved over time, examined trends related to framing and language usage, and assess whether a distinction exists between national and local perspectives. Our research reveals notable patterns, including varied coverage of personal stories and health information across national, local, and virtual platforms, and hints of relatedness between the language used in local reporting and community discussions on social media platforms.

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, children gradually transition from representing quantities with one type of symbol to systematically using two types of symbols. While a wide range of non-human species demonstrate an ability to count small numbers of objects, only humans have shown a capacity for exactly counting a large number of objects, mastering the system of counting that involves switching between two symbols. In this study, we provide the first evidence that the difficulty of learning to count peaks when children are just beginning to develop this skill and shows that there are significant differences between cultures in when (or if) children learn to count. Children from the U.S., a culture with a system of counting that involves three symbols, were easier to train to count four than ten on average. In contrast, Xhosa children, a culture that develops a system of counting that involves five symbols, found it just as difficult to count four as ten. Our results provide a precise point of reference for the cognitive development of learning to count and reveal that there are cultural differences in when (or if) children learn to count.

A well-respected data structure, the cuckoo filter, evolves from the popular Bloom filter concept, offering a compact way to efficiently test whether elements belong to a specified set. It outperforms Bloom filters by significantly reducing space requirements while maintaining comparable error rates. However, addressing false positives takes longer with the cuckoo filter. This paper proposes an improved version of the cuckoo filter that eliminates extra steps in verifying elements and elements from the original set by integrating a pointer-based approach. The modified filter stores either a single bit or one integer per entry for marking occupied slots. Our research indicates that the updated method can produce the same results as the original filter but with faster performance.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our focus is on establishing a framework for translating concepts and proofs from convex geometry to K\"ahler geometry, with minimal reliance on specific features of K\"ahler manifolds. This approach generalizes existing comparisons between positive products and mixed volumes or Dirichlet polynomials and zeta functions. As an example, we derive a relationship linking line bundles with their associated (singular) Hermitian metrics to convex bodies and support functions.

A new approach aims to derive market trend indicators from trade volume data, specifically how many shares are traded within a set time frame. Existing indicators, such as MACD or RSI, don't consider this metric in their calculations. Research found that trade volume can significantly impact future stock prices, leading to an experimental rate-indicator. This is described as a weighted sum of trade volumes, where weights are stock price inverses. An analysis of this indicator and its potential prediction ability is presented, focusing on its performance in the stock market of India. An initial evaluation was conducted using the Shapley value to measure the predictor ability. Results indicated high prediction accuracy for shorter time frames and when analyzing rate indicators related to trading during working hours. An extreme gradient boosting model was employed to predict the direction of stock price movement. This model was optimized by selecting the optimal time lag and combining rate indicators with WMA, a volume-weighted average price indicator. Outcome measures, such as profit and loss and the Kelker performance index, were found to indicate a model capable of making profitable predictions and correctly predicting price movements. Outcome indicators proposed stock selection as a more practical application. Results indicated high performance when using time lag of 5, 15, and 30 minutes, with model capabilities to correctly predict the direction of stock prices.

This study presents FLVoigdt, a federated learning framework that incorporates decentralized voting to safeguard local models against Byzantine attacks while maintaining user privacy. The proposed method enables collaborative voting on model reliability without disclosing individual model details, leveraging the power of homomorphic encryption and secret sharing protocols. Our research demonstrates that FLVoigdt effectively prevents malicious behavior, detects attacking clients with high accuracy and ensures private communication between clients and the server. Furthermore, the server's safe aggregation of local models using SMIR allows it to gradually improve its knowledge of safe model selection, allowing it to distinguish between safe and malicious models, ultimately leading to faster detection. Additionally, our clinical trial results show that FLVoigdt produces higher clinical performance compared to existing methods, making it a promising solution for real-world federated learning applications.

We successfully demonstrate a significant advancement in using a reinforcement learning agent to learn optimal driving strategies in simulated environments. Through developing and implementing novel training techniques, the agent is able to learn complex behaviors that surpass the capabilities of existing autonomous driving methods in difficult situations. Key innovations in our method involve increasing training efficiency by factor of 100 using targeted data selection, improving policy robustability through control transformation, and enhancing the training stability by factoring in the effects of sensor noise and system delays. When combined with an existing autonomous driving method, our technique consistently produces superior results and significantly reduces the required training time. We note that although reinforcement learning offers substantial potential for developing safe and efficient driving behavior, there remains the challenge of significantly reducing the amount of time needed for training.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications such as film and television production, voice restoration, voice authentication, and robotics. Notably, the field of deepfake research has made significant strides in creating high-quality deepfake videos and voices based on existing datasets, including face swapping and voice conversion techniques. This paper aims to provide an in-depth examination of deepfake technology, starting with an overview of key concepts in deep learning and its relevance to deepfake research. Subsequently, the paper will explore the specific techniques used in generating deepfake videos and voices, as well as the potential applications and ethical implications associated with this technology.

The identification of a significant number of sub-Neptune exoplanets has led to a pressing necessity to develop an understanding of their internal structures and capabilities to sustain habitable environments with liquid water oceans on or beneath their surfaces. Researchers have been investigating how factors such as stellar metallicity, which influences the supply of volatiles for planet formation, and core superrotation, which affects atmospheric dynamics and the maintenance of liquid oceans, influence the potential habitability of these exoplanets. A study, focused on K2-18 b, shows that variations in stellar metallicity produce a broad range of potential habitable worlds with H2O-rich surfaces. However, core superrotation significantly impacts the potential for liquid surface oceans, particularly for closely spaced planets and those with high temperatures. Therefore, further observations and simulations are required to fully assess the potential for habitable environments on low-mass exoplanets.

Inspired by the famous McCulloch-Pitts binary neuron, this study explores a novel model of sparse learning that mimics the properties of binary neurons. It discovers that the model requires connections between neurons to be asymmetric in order to create sequences. Furthermore, the study shows that the correlation between connections and sequences improves as the degree of asymmetry increases. Notably, the learning model fails when connections are symmetric. Our findings are confirmed by two complex neuronal networks with opposing levels of connection asymmetry, which exhibit distinct differences in their ability to learn sequences. The study's results emphasize the significance of asymmetric connections in neural systems for sequence learning, providing insight into the characteristics of sparse neural networks.

This study introduces a novel approach to training scene text OCR models by leveraging real-world images. Unlike conventional methods that require pre-selecting training images, our method can learn from any real-world images, regardless of the text content they contain. However, obscuring text in images often results in models encountering unseen OCR text during training, which negatively affects their recognition capabilities for this type of text. Our method tackles this issue by introducing a novel character-based loss function that simultaneously models character-level dependencies and class probabilities. By doing so, our model achieves superior OCR accuracy compared to existing models when trained on real-world images.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates generalized polynomial chaos methods by applying it in a spatial context rather than time or simultaneously in multiple dimensions. Also, a relevant set of basis functions is developed that accommodates boundary conditions without loss of orthogonality, and efficient projection techniques are proposed that consider these functions along with boundary constraints. Finally, several test cases involving generalized polynomial chaos expansions are presented to demonstrate the approach's potential for solving one-dimensional spatial stochastic differential equations.

The increasing prevalence of industrial applications has led to a significant rise in the demand for monitoring complex, high-dimensional data sets. Notably, the data characteristics such as non-stationarity, noise, multicollinearity, and high dimensionality pose substantial challenges for effective process monitoring. This study addresses these challenges by integrating the non-parametric smoothed scatterplot technique with a dimension reduction method called Orthogonal Partial Least Squares. The proposed framework enables the development of a non-parametric monitoring system that can effectively track both individual process variables and overall process performance. The potential of this technique is demonstrated through a numerical simulation example and a real-world case involving the monitoring of paper machine calender rolls temperature.

We have created a detailed analysis of the Milky Way's accreted galaxies Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 by charting their presence in early Milky Way structures. The analysis includes calculating infall timescales and examining their potential host structures. The results show GSE's infall timescale to be approximately 3.5 billion years, with a similar scale of around 3.3 billion years for a structure that may have fed GSE. LMS-1's infall timescale is around 4.5-5.5 billion years, exhibiting a similar pattern with a smaller structure that fell in around 3.5-4.5 billion years. Another structure that may have contributed to LMS-1's growth, termed Wukong, fell in around a 3.5-4.5 billion years ago. Comparing our calculations with previous studies on M32 quiescent galaxies reveals GSE, LMS-1, and the unnamed structure dubbed Wukong are part of a broader phenomenon.

Given a profinite group G, an S[[G]]-module is a supersingular spectrum of finitely presented G-spectrum action, resulting in a finitely presented pro-spectrum of G-spectrum action. This allows for the computation of the continuous homology of a profinite group G, as well as the homotopy orbit spectral sequence of a S[[G]]-module M at an odd prime p. If M satisfies a finiteness condition, the convergence of the homotopy orbit spectral sequence can be established.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a quantum spin Hall system. Initially formed with a 0.1 eV valence band offset (InAs maximum higher than EuS), our studies using first principles calculations explored four different bonding configurations to understand how this offset arises. We found that for an interface stabilized by ferroagnetic ordering, two configurations exhibit a intrinsic 0.1-0.2 eV offset, while two others exhibit offset values close to zero. Importantly, all four configurations are compatible with other EuS interface elements and allow for the preservation of Eu magnetic ordering. Our results imply that a significant band offset can form without requiring lattice mismatch or magnetic disorder, providing a basis for building stable quantum magnetic spintronics devices.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are increasingly being used for various tasks, but they come with high inference costs. The recent surge in neural machine translation models using self attention mechanisms has also highlighted the issue of high computational costs during both training and inference. We developed ClickTrain, a parallel framework to efficiently train CNNs on a single GPU by leveraging the intersection of interest labels and predicted positives. ClickTrain's design enables the synchronized computation of forward passes and data loading in mini-batches, thus maximizing the utilization of available resources. ClickTrain's performance demonstration on cross-lingual machine mining tasks reveals a 4 times speedup on GPU, making it possible to train models larger than previously allowed by a given GPU's memory capacity.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a specific structural rule. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model developed from Priestley spaces.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and the Pulsar Timing Array have identified three distinct types of merging compact binaries: black holes fusing, black holes interacting with neutron stars, and neutron stars interacting with each other, all of which generate gravitational waves. These events can be categorized into those occurring at shorter distances, whose frequencies fall within the range of ground-based detectors, and those from further away, whose low frequencies allow them to be picked up by solar system-based observers. Over a period of approximately six years, the International Pulsar Timing Array has been collecting precision data on the arrival times of radio pulses from five carefully selected stars, which has set stringent limits on the amplitude of possible gravitational waves. Our research demonstrates that these limits rule out certain astrophysical models describing the formation of stellar-mass black holes in the universe.

A new discovery has been made about a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around an active sun-like star that belongs to a relatively old group of stars known as the Hyades. Initially identified as a candidate by the TESS mission and the NEOWISE partnership, which utilizes infrared data from the Wide Field Camera on the WISE satellite to identify suitable targets, this exoplanet, which has a minimum mass equivalent to 1.17 times that of Jupiter, was subsequently confirmed through radial velocity measurements by the HARPS, FERVE, and HARPS-N spectrographs. Notably, this discovery is significant because it belongs to a particular category of exoplanets, which are gas giants that orbit close to their host stars, and it is located far from our solar system, at a distance of 4.5 lightyears. Although there has been an established connection between metal-rich stars and planets that have greater masses, this connection is not present in the case of this particular system, which is unusual because the host star of this exoplanet has low metal content and it is part of a cluster that is known to be metal-poor. Consequently, this discovery challenges the previously held notion that the presence of metal in a star is a prerequisite for the formation of large gas giants, especially those that orbit close to their host stars. This new finding is consistent with the hypothesis that these giant exoplanets can be created through the process of core collapse, which is a type of gravitational

Sequential decision-making problems under restrictions, such as those found in operations management, marketing, and networking, are typically addressed using constrained Markov decision processes. Traditional solution methods for these problems involve approximating their structure with either policy iteration or value iteration, developing closed-form solutions, or Monte Carlo simulation. However, these approaches have their own drawbacks - high computational costs, inaccurate results, or failing to fully utilize the problem's underlying structure. We present a novel value iteration approach that utilizes Newton's method to efficiently solve the normal form linear programming representation of the problem. This formulation incorporates the problem's monotonically decreasing returns to scale property to reduce its size. We also propose an additional formulation that balances accuracy and efficiency, allowing the options to be tailored according to the desired trade-off between computation time and solution precision. We thoroughly evaluate our algorithm and demonstrate its advantages over a range of competitors on several test cases. Subsequently, we leverage this improved value iteration method to create a more efficient iterative policy improvement approach. We apply both value iteration and iterative policy improvement to a range of practical scenarios to showcase their performance in real-world applications.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols, starting with the task of segmenting these symbols. Since many complex mathematical expressions can be difficult to decompose, our approach focuses on simplifying this task. We introduce a new dataset, SDGML, consisting of 1,385 mathematical symbols, each presented in various forms and backgrounds. To increase the complexity of our study, we include 9,805 DLMLML images, which depict multiple symbols combined. The hand drawn nature of this data demands a flexible input, leading us to test multiple segmentation techniques. These methods range from traditional handwritten recognition to more advanced language model-based approaches. Our analysis focuses on the effectiveness of these methods when applied to complex mathematical expressions. The MSDML project is another key component of this dataset, which is an ML platform for mathematical symbol recognition, starting with the segmentation task.

A geometric interpretation of superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler manifold's resolved singularities has an established connection to topological twisted Dolbeault cohomology. Building upon this relationship, our work derives an equation linking supercharges to twisted holomorphic vector field generators, which in turn demonstrates that BPS states correspond to twisted Dolbeault cohomology classes. Furthermore, an additive indexing technique for these BPS states has been developed based on rational BPS charges, with specific calculations for the harmonic oscillator providing an explicit table of these states.

We investigate the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical simulations. Our research reveals that the heterogeneous network type significantly impacts the final disease prevalence, whereas in homogeneous networks, the prevalence mainly depends on the disease transmissibility. Additionally, we examine how the critical disease transmissibility varies based on the network configuration, noting that the heterogeneity of the network influences this critical threshold. Notably, we observe distinct critical values for heterogeneous networks, marking the transition between low and high prevalence states. We further explore the critical exponent associated with this critical threshold, discovering that this exponent is an intrinsic property of the contact process and is sensitive to the network architecture. Architecting the network to minimize extreme nodes results in a shift of the critical disease transmissibility towards higher values. Conversely, increasing the amount of extreme nodes leads to a lower critical disease transmissibility. The best fit for this critical shift as a function of the power of the degree distribution yields an exponent of approximately -2.1, consistent with previous theory.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is often constrained by the exploratory abilities of its architectures, which can hinder progress toward the optimal policy. To overcome this limitation, a new technique allows the critic component to draw a broader range of target states through the hybridization of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and actor-critic reinforcement learning. This integration enhances the critic's ability to discover optimal policy parameters, as it facilitates the discovery of previously unnoticed target states. Experimental evaluations have demonstrated that actor-critic reinforcement learning method enriched with the HMC-based critic consistently achieves better results, outperforming its counterpart, especially in more difficult tasks. Furthermore, this technique shows particularly notable improvements when the actor-critic reinforcement learning method employs particularly exploratory architectures. Notably, our findings indicate that the HMC-critic effectively compensates for reduced architectural exploration, thus yielding results comparable to its counterpart, which employs highly exploratory architectures.

It's widely known that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$ for a natural number $k$. We will explore the relationship that any such prime $p$ satisfies, specifically $p=6k-p_{j}^i$, where the natural number $k$ is calculated as $\frac{p+1}{6}$, and $p_{j}$ is a prime that is the $i$-th smallest prime such that $p_{i} < p$. We will also examine how this relationship can be applied in the field of cryptography.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots, particularly when outdoor weather factors like rain or snow also impact their ability to detect text, patterns, and textures using standard sensors. Moreover, indoor environments often lack consistent features for the robot to recognize, hindering its ability to identify its location. This research introduces a novel multimodal fusion technique, combining air image data with visible light text, to optimize pattern matching text recognition. The proposed method utilizes the low-level air image to enhance the middle-level feature extraction, boosting the overall accuracy of the fusion. With a dataset of air images and a visible light camera integrated into the ASU LMS MARS mobile robot, experimental results show improved navigation performance in both indoor and outdoor settings.
